# Three-cap overlap in every ordinary continuous dimension

This note concerns ordinary continuous convex bodies. Its projective measure is an integral over all real coordinates, not a sampled mixed-integer measure. It does not assert a projective transformation preserves the mixed lattice.

## Theorem

Let K be a convex body in R^D, D>=2. Let H_1,H_2,H_3 be closed halfspaces whose union contains K. Put V=vol_D(K), A_i=vol_D(K intersect H_i). Then

    A_1+A_2+A_3-V >= (3/4) min_i A_i.                 (1)

There is no restriction on the rank of the three normals. The constant is sharp: a triangle with its three canonical centroid caps, times an arbitrary positive-volume convex body in R^(D-2), has equality.

The planar uniform-body case was proved in `candidate e239a5fb0d0efe4d` and its arbitrary-cover companion. This note reduces all dimensions to that established case. The rank-two portion also has an independently authored direct proof in `candidate afc7b749e1d0fe7a`.

## 1. An inverse-power radial-integral lemma

Let r>=1 and beta>=r+1. Let f be a finite positive-integral density on R^r with an open full-dimensional convex positive set U, and suppose phi=f^(-1/beta) is finite positive and convex on U. Set f=0 outside U; boundary values do not affect any integrals. If 0 belongs to U, then

    I(x)=integral_0^infinity t^(r-1) f(tx) dt,
    q(x)=I(x)^(-1/r)       (x!=0),     q(0)=0

defines a finite continuous convex positively homogeneous function. Its unit sublevel is a convex body containing zero in its interior.

Here are the needed bounds, including tails. On a small ball about zero, phi is bounded above, and f is bounded below by a positive constant. Also inf_U phi>0. Otherwise, if phi(x_j)=epsilon_j decreases to zero, mix x_j with a fixed ball on which phi<=A using the proportion theta_j=epsilon_j/A. On the resulting ball of radius proportional to epsilon_j, phi<=2epsilon_j. Its f-integral is at least a positive constant times epsilon_j^(r-beta), which tends to infinity and contradicts the fixed finite total integral.

The convex sublevel {phi<=2phi(0)} contains a ball and has finite volume, because f is bounded below there. It is bounded: an unbounded convex set containing a ball contains cones with arbitrarily large volume. Choose R enclosing that sublevel. Convexity along a ray from zero then gives, for x in U with |x|>=R,

    phi(x)>=phi(0)(1+|x|/R).

After enlarging a constant on the remaining bounded region, this proves

    f(x)<=C(1+|x|)^(-beta).                              (2)

Thus I is positive finite and uniformly bounded above and below on the unit sphere. It is continuous there by dominated convergence: along a ray from an interior point, all but at most one parameter are interior or exterior to the closure of U. The bound (2) is integrable against t^(r-1), since beta>r.

To prove convexity, take x,y with I(x)=I(y)=1 and 0<lambda<1. Couple the positive ray densities t^(r-1)f(tx) and t^(r-1)f(ty) by their increasing quantiles R(v),S(v), 0<v<1. They are continuously differentiable on this interval and

    R'=1/[R^(r-1) f(Rx)],    S'=1/[S^(r-1) f(Sy)].

For z=lambda x+(1-lambda)y define

    T=(lambda/R+(1-lambda)/S)^(-1),
    a=lambda T/R,    b=(1-lambda)T/S.

Then a,b>0, a+b=1, T=aR+bS, and Tz=aRx+bSy. Write X=f(Rx)^(-1/beta), Y=f(Sy)^(-1/beta). Convexity of phi gives f(Tz)>=(aX+bY)^(-beta). Differentiating T yields

    T^(r-1) f(Tz) T'
      >= T^r [a X^beta/R^r+b Y^beta/S^r]/(aX+bY)^beta.

Weighted Holder followed by concavity of t^(r/(beta-1)) gives

    (aX+bY)^beta
      <= [a X^beta/R^r+b Y^beta/S^r]
         [a R^(r/(beta-1))+b S^(r/(beta-1))]^(beta-1)
      <= [a X^beta/R^r+b Y^beta/S^r] T^r.

The exponent lies in (0,1] precisely because beta>=r+1. Hence the preceding integrand is at least one. T increases strictly from zero. Integrating in v gives I(z)>=1. Positive homogeneity, the uniform radial bounds, and continuity now show that the unit sublevel is a convex body and q its convex gauge.

In particular the radial body B defined by

    rho_B(u)^r=r integral_0^infinity t^(r-1) f(tu) dt

has volume integral f. Polar integration shows that it has exactly the same mass as f in EVERY through-zero halfspace. The lemma applies after translating any interior point of U to zero; there is no mode or centroid assumption.

This is a direct nonsymmetric proof of the needed inverse-power extension of Ball's radial construction. Ordinary background on this extension is Bobkov, *Convex bodies and norms associated to convex measures*, Sections 2--3, https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~bobko001/papers/2010_PTRF_Norms.pdf. The proof above does not borrow a symmetry assumption from that paper's displayed norm theorem.

## 2. Three-cap overlap for inverse-cubic planar densities

Let f on R^2 satisfy Section 1 with beta=3, and let three closed halfplanes cover the whole plane and have a minimal positive circuit of normals. Then (1) holds with f-masses in place of volumes.

Zero or full cap mass is immediate by the union bound or by summing the other two masses. For three proper caps, apply common-upper-level cap tightening from `candidate d2f8ecd6d2f1309c`, with r there equal to 3/4. Its proof works for this density as follows. Every cap tail is continuous, and strictly decreasing between proper levels because f is positive on the interior of its convex support. Thus proper quantile thresholds exist and are continuous. As a common upper mass level tends to zero, every threshold eventually exceeds the scalar product of its normal with any fixed interior support point. The positive weighted threshold sum is then positive. The same intermediate value and functional monotonicity proof therefore gives smaller, concurrent caps whose functional sum A_i-(3/4)min A_i is no larger.

Let y be their concurrence point. If y is outside or on the boundary of the convex support, that support lies in a closed halfplane through y. At most two of the three concurrent halfplanes cover that halfplane: on its angular interval of length pi, retain the longest initial and terminal covering intervals. The third cap contributes at least the minimum to the total overlap, so the desired coefficient 3/4 follows.

If y is in the positive interior, use the radial body of Section 1 about y. It is a planar convex body with the same total mass and exactly the same three through-y cap masses. The already proved planar uniform-body theorem gives the result. Common-level tightening then returns it to the original halfplanes. Equivalently, the planar uniform-body input now has the short independent distal-truncation proof in `candidate cd833c78fb705a2e`.

## 3. The precise marginal theorem used below

We use the standard Borell--Brascamp--Lieb marginal implication: if G is a nonnegative integrable function of (z,w), with w in R^k, its positive support is convex, and G^p is convex for a negative p>-1/k, then F(z)=integral G(z,w) dw has F^(p/(1+kp)) convex on its positive support. The inequalities are understood only at positive endpoint values; zero values outside the convex support are permitted.

This follows by applying the usual functional BBL inequality to two w-sections and their interpolated section. A precise primary statement is Lemma 2.3 of Bobkov's paper linked above, with k as its integration dimension and kappa=p/(1+kp). No mixed-integer statement is involved. When k=0 there is no integration and the assertion is the original convexity condition.

## 4. A projective marginal of ordinary uniform volume

Suppose D>=3 and affine coordinates on R^D have been chosen as (v,t,y), with v in R^2 and y in R^(D-3), so that K lies in {t>=0}. Assume t is nonconstant; hence t>0 throughout int(K). The zero-t boundary has D-volume zero. Push ordinary uniform volume forward by

    (v,t,y) -> z=v/t       on t>0.

Ignoring the fixed positive affine-coordinate Jacobian, which is restored as one scalar factor, its density is

    F(z)=integral_(t>0) integral_y 1_K(tz,t,y) t^2 dy dt.     (3)

It is finite and bounded because K is bounded, so both t and y range in fixed bounded sets. Its positive support is full-dimensional. Its total mass is V, after restoring the coordinate Jacobian.

Set s=1/t, w=y/t. Formula (3) becomes

    F(z)=integral 1_Omega(z,s,w) s^(-(D+1)) ds dw,

where s>0 and

    Omega={(z,s,w):(z/s,1/s,w/s) belongs to K}.

The domain Omega is convex. Indeed a convex combination of two (z,s,w) corresponds, in the original coordinates, to a convex combination with weights proportional to their positive s coordinates. The integrand raised to the power -1/(D+1) is exactly s on Omega, and therefore convex there. There are D-2 integrated variables. Applying Section 3 with p=-1/(D+1) gives

    p/(1+(D-2)p)=-1/3.

Thus F^(-1/3) is convex on its positive support. Replace F on the boundary of that full-dimensional convex support by zero and use its open interior as U; the boundary is Lebesgue-null, so every cap and total mass is unchanged. The fixed positive coordinate factor does not affect this property. All halfspaces whose boundaries contain the plane {v=t=0} become ordinary affine halfplanes in z, with their volume fractions preserved exactly. This calculation works whether that common plane meets K or lies outside it.

## 5. Proof of the theorem

If any two caps cover K, then A_1+A_2+A_3-V is at least the mass of the remaining cap and hence at least min A_i. Assume no two cover K. Zero and full cap cases are already immediate, so retain only proper positive caps.

If the normals span a line, a two-cap subcover exists: restrictions to the projected interval are half-lines, and at most one cap of each orientation is needed. This contradicts the current assumption.

If the normal rank is two, project ordinary volume orthogonally onto their plane. Its density is log-concave, by ordinary section Brunn--Minkowski or Prekopa. Hence its inverse cube root is convex on its positive support. Planar Helly applied to that support and the three open cap complements shows that either two caps cover the support or the three halfplanes cover the whole plane. The former case was excluded. Their normals are consequently a minimal positive circuit, and Section 2 applies. This proves (1) in the rank-two case.

Finally suppose the normal rank is three, so D>=3. The affine margin map

    x -> (a_1.x-b_1, a_2.x-b_2, a_3.x-b_3)

has rank three and maps K to a full-dimensional compact convex set Q in R^3. Q is disjoint from the open negative orthant. Convex separation therefore supplies lambda_i>=0, not all zero, such that

    sum_i lambda_i m_i>=0       for every m in Q.

For precision, finiteness of the supremum of the separating functional on the negative orthant forces the coefficients to be nonnegative, and that supremum is zero. If any coefficient were zero, the caps with positive coefficients would already cover K, producing a two-cap subcover. Thus every lambda_i is positive.

Use affine coordinates (v,t,y) in which the three original margins are homogeneous linear forms L_i(v,t), and

    t=sum_i lambda_i L_i(v,t).

Such coordinates exist by the rank-three assumption. K lies in {t>=0}, and the projective marginal F of Section 4 preserves all three cap masses. The image halfplanes are

    L_i(z,1)>=0.

Their positive weighted sum is identically one, so they cover the entire plane. Their planar normals span dimension two and have a minimal positive dependence: otherwise the three original homogeneous forms would have rank at most two. The marginal is inverse-cubic convex, so Section 2 proves (1).

Every case has now been treated. The proof used only ordinary D-volume and genuine changes of real integration variables. It has no implication that sampled projective fiber laws satisfy this concavity; explicit archived mixed-integer counterexamples to that separate assertion remain in force.
